elements.element: Customer has no non-compete or field-of-use restriction.
elements.evidence: The offending second § 12.4 ("During the term and for twenty-four months thereafter, Customer shall not develop, market, sell, or acquire any product or service that competes with Vendor in any territory") is gone from the rendered text and replaced by: "12.4 Customer is subject to no non-compete or field-of-use restriction, and may develop, market, sell, or acquire any product or service, including any that competes with Vendor, in any territory." No other customer-binding compete, field-of-use or territory covenant survives (the deterministic check "no open-ended compete restriction on Customer remains" returns ok), and § 12.3's confirmation that Customer made "no exclusivity, non-compete ... commitment" is retained.

elements.element: The restriction covers only a named competing product.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: after the edit there is no restriction on Customer at all, so a fortiori nothing broader than a single named competing product binds us (rendered § 12.4 affirms Customer "may develop, market, sell, or acquire any product or service, including any that competes with Vendor").

elements.element: The restriction applies during the term only.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the post-term "and for twenty-four months thereafter" tail was struck along with the covenant, so no obligation extends past the term (or exists during it).

elements.element: The restriction lasts no longer than 12 months.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: with the covenant deleted there is no duration to cap; the 24-month period no longer appears in the operative text.

elements.element: The restriction permits Customer's internal development.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: rendered § 12.4 expressly confirms Customer "may develop ... any product or service," and § 12.3 (retained) states "Nothing restricts Customer from developing ... any product or service."

Condition does not apply: rendered § 12.4 confirms Customer may "acquire any product or service, including any that competes with Vendor, in any territory," and § 12.3 preserves the same freedom to acquire.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: the sole preferred element is met in operative language, not merely promised in the comment — the 24-month, all-territory covenant is removed and replaced with an affirmative confirmation that no non-compete or field-of-use restriction binds Customer.

The fallback checklist is satisfied vacuously because no restriction remains; every fallback element is a constraint on a restriction whose condition no longer exists, and the fallback (term-only, single named product, 12 months, development/acquisition carve-outs) is correctly reserved to the margin comment rather than being drafted into the operative text.

Minimality holds: only the offending second § 12.4 sentence was touched; customer-favourable § 12.3 is retained verbatim, the separate no-hire covenant in the first § 12.4 is left for its own rule, and Vendor-side restrictions (e.g. the § 24.2 assignment limit) are untouched. No new obligations, fees, or timing mechanics are introduced.

Nit only, not a defect: the replacement sentence largely restates § 12.3's existing acknowledgement, so there is mild duplication of operative content. A tighter edit would be to strike the sentence outright (or mark § 12.4 "[Intentionally omitted]") and rely on § 12.3; because the restatement imposes no obligation and does not conflict with § 12.3, it does not break minimality or intent.

No internal inconsistency created: the new § 12.4 addresses only products/services, territory and field of use, so it does not silently override the first § 12.4's no-hire covenant. Note for the drafter that the pre-existing tension between that no-hire covenant and § 12.3's "no ... no-hire commitment" language is untouched here and should be resolved under the no-hire rule.

Both walk-away triggers were present in the original (post-term restriction of 24 months and undefined scope, "any product or service that competes with Vendor in any territory"), so the "deviation" characterisation with the preferred-level strike is the right call; the edit fully cures both. Severity remains high per the rule.
